overview: Chorus is New Zealand's largest fixed-line telecommunications infrastructure company, built through the government-backed Ultra-Fast Broadband (UFB) public-private partnership completed in the early-to-mid 2020s. It operates a wholesale-only, open-access fibre (and now almost fully retired legacy copper) network covering roughly 84% of New Zealand's fibre footprint (the rest served by three smaller Local Fibre Companies), selling connectivity to around 90 retail service providers (Spark, One NZ/Vodafone, 2degrees, and smaller ISPs) rather than to end consumers directly. As a regulated natural monopoly, Chorus' fibre revenues, allowed returns and capital spend are set by the Commerce Commission under a Price-Quality Path (PQ) building-blocks/RAB regime, with the second regulatory period (PQ2) running 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2028 and preparatory work for PQ3 (from 2029) already underway via the 2027 Fibre Input Methodologies Review.

business_model.summary: Chorus earns regulated, largely fixed monthly wholesale access fees from retail service providers for fibre (GPON/P2P) and now near-extinct copper connections. Revenue is highly recurring (subscription-like wholesale access charges) with a growing high-speed/high-ARPU mix as customers upgrade plans and migrate off copper. The completed UFB build means capital expenditure has stepped down from build-era peaks (~$650-670m p.a.) to a sustaining/growth capex base of $375m in FY26, with FY27 guided at $375-415m, turning Chorus into a free-cash-flow-generative, high-payout infrastructure/income stock (FY26 free cash flow for capital allocation of $368m, up 4% on FY25's $354m).

revenue_streams.name: Field services / infrastructure / VANS / other
revenue_streams.trend: stable, with new data-centre-adjacent products (Express Connect, Unified Transport, TimeSync) emerging

business_model.customer_type: B2B wholesale-only; sells to ~90 retail service providers (Spark, One NZ, 2degrees, and smaller ISPs) who in turn serve NZ residential and business end customers. Chorus has no direct retail relationship or brand-facing role with consumers.
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand. Nationwide fixed-line network with over 1.1 million fibre connections at FY26 year-end (fibre uptake 75.9%, UFB1 areas 77.3%, UFB2 areas 67.5%), covering most of the country outside three Local Fibre Company (LFC) regions (Enable/Christchurch, Northpower/Whangarei, Tuatahi First Fibre/Waikato rural). Copper lines in Chorus' fibre zone are now fewer than 1,000, effectively at end-of-life.

main_competitors: Starlink and other LEO satellite broadband
competitive_position.market_position: Regulated monopoly wholesaler across ~84% of the UFB fibre footprint (the remainder split among three smaller Local Fibre Companies under the same PQ regulatory framework); no fibre-on-fibre overbuild competition within its own footprint, but faces growing inter-technology competition (FWA, LEO satellite) for connections, especially rural/low-density areas and the low end of the market. Starlink has become NZ's largest single rural broadband provider by connections (27% of rural broadband share per the Commerce Commission's 2025 Telecommunications Monitoring Report, up from 19% a year earlier, ahead of Spark at 23% and One NZ at 18%), underscoring that competition now matters even where fibre is available, not just at the fringe.

moat_factors.factor: Regulated natural monopoly / high barriers to entry
moat_factors.description: Duplicating a nationwide fibre network is capital-prohibitive; Chorus is the default wholesale fibre provider across most of NZ with Commerce Commission-set, cost-recovery-based revenue via the RAB, giving highly visible, government-sanctioned cash flows.

moat_factors.factor: Essential-service switching costs at the wholesale layer
moat_factors.description: Retail service providers are effectively captive to whichever network passes a given address; end customers rarely have a same-cost, same-speed fixed alternative to fibre once available, and fibre is increasingly viewed as an essential utility. Monthly data usage per fibre connection rose 9% in FY26 to 731GB, reinforcing fibre's capacity advantage as AI/streaming/data-centre-adjacent demand grows.

PQ2 (2025-2028) sets allowed revenue off a RAB split into a Core RAB and a Financial Loss Asset that rolls forward with approved capex and an allowed WACC, giving multi-year revenue/cash-flow visibility uncommon among industrials. The 2027 Fibre Input Methodologies Review (Tranche 1 final decision package published 25 August 2026) is now setting the groundwork for PQ3 (from 2029); notably, the Commission's preliminary analysis found a marked reduction in the assessed systematic risk of fibre businesses, which -- all else equal -- points toward a LOWER allowed WACC in PQ3 than PQ2, a swing factor investors should watch (Tranche 2, covering fibre-specific cost of capital, and the cross-sector common cost-of-capital IM review are due to conclude separately, with final cost-of-capital parameters expected Q4 2026).

moat_factors.factor: Network scale and cost position vs FWA/satellite
moat_factors.description: Fibre offers materially higher speed, lower latency, and better reliability/economics per GB than 5G FWA or LEO satellite at high usage levels, supporting continued uptake growth even as those technologies erode the addressable market at the margin, particularly in rural areas where Starlink has overtaken traditional telcos on share.

weaknesses: Zero pricing power outside the regulator-approved framework — Chorus cannot raise prices or reallocate capital freely; upside is capped by regulatory determinations, and the Commission's own risk analysis for PQ3 currently points toward a lower allowed return, not a higher one

Structural decline (now near-complete) of copper revenue as customers migrate to fibre or alternative technologies; copper lines disconnected fell 52% (48,000 lines) in FY26 alone, with fewer than 1,000 remaining in Chorus' fibre zone and full national retirement targeted by end of 2028
No brand or direct customer relationship — entirely dependent on retail service providers' marketing, pricing and bundling decisions to drive connections and ARPU

High leverage (net debt/EBITDA ~4.5x at HY26, net debt of $3.2bn at FY26 year-end, up $72m YoY) built up during the UFB build years constrains discretionary capital allocation and dividend flexibility if rates or EBITDA disappoint; total equity was $430m at 31 December 2025 (down from $567m at 30 June 2025 and $841m at 1 July 2024) against total debt (current + non-current) of roughly $3.34bn

Mature-market ceiling and share erosion at the margin: fibre uptake reached 75.9% by FY26 year-end (UFB2/rural areas lag at 67.5%), and Starlink has already overtaken Spark and One NZ to become the largest rural broadband provider by connections, showing substitution is a present-day headwind, not just a future risk

growth_drivers: Continued fibre uptake growth (75.9% at FY26 year-end, up from 72.4% at HY26 and management's prior ~80%-by-2030 target), adding high-margin incremental connections onto an already-built network, though the 'last 25%' (rural/UFB2) is proving harder-won against FWA/satellite competition
ARPU growth from plan mix-shift to higher speed tiers (gigabit/multi-gigabit ~25% of the base) and CPI/inflation-linked regulated price increases; FY26 ARPU rose ~2% to $59.51/month

Completed copper withdrawal programme cutting network maintenance, electricity and operating costs; full national copper retirement targeted by end of 2028 (rural/non-fibre areas), with fibre-zone copper already down to fewer than 1,000 lines; a new copper-recycling initiative is contributing incremental EBITDA (~$4m in FY26, an estimated $50-70m cumulative return through 2030)
Post-UFB capex step-down (from ~$650-670m p.a. build-era peak to $375m actual gross capex in FY26, guided $375-415m for FY27) mechanically expanding free cash flow available for dividends

New/adjacent revenue lines targeting the AI/data-centre boom: Express Connect (operational in 8 data centres), Unified Transport, TimeSync (precision timing, entered build phase), and Hyperfibre (premium gigabit-plus product targeting 70,000 connections by 2030); a potential inter-island subsea cable (estimated $60-80m capex over 3 years) and battery energy storage trials are early-stage optionality (the previously-explored Trans-Tasman Ring project was shelved in FY26/HY26 and is no longer being actively pursued)

PQ2 regulatory settlement (2025-2028) providing multi-year revenue and capex allowance certainty, supporting the high (70-90% of net operating FCF) dividend payout policy set in FY24; FY27 minimum dividend guidance of 62 cents/share (up 3.3% on FY26's 60 cents) is now expected to carry partial imputation credits, an incremental positive for NZ resident shareholders

Commerce Commission deregulation of copper services outside fibre areas (recommended 2025) removing compliance costs and TSO-style obligations for the shrinking rural copper footprint faster than expected, and allowing Chorus to bring forward full retirement to 2028 from the prior 2030 target

business.risk: Fixed wireless access (FWA) and satellite (Starlink) competition
business.description: Starlink has already overtaken Spark and One NZ to become New Zealand's largest rural broadband provider by connections (27% share per the Commerce Commission's 2025 Telecommunications Monitoring Report, up from 19% the prior year); low-usage and price-sensitive/rural customers increasingly bypass fibre entirely, capping the uptake ceiling (UFB2/rural areas lag at 67.5% uptake vs 77.3% in UFB1) and pressuring low-end ARPU. The Commerce Commission itself cited this substitution as the basis for recommending copper deregulation, and its own September 2026 commentary frames competition as now mattering 'even inside areas where fibre is available.'

Uptake reached 75.9% by FY26 year-end; each incremental point of uptake becomes harder to win as remaining prospects are disproportionately price-sensitive, rural, or already served by an alternative technology -- underscored by an industry commentary piece (Sept 2026) framing the 'last 25%' of the rollout as structurally different and harder than the first 75%.

business.risk: Retail service provider concentration and behaviour
business.description: Chorus has no direct end-customer relationship; volume and ARPU depend on Spark, One NZ and 2degrees' retail pricing, bundling and marketing choices.

Growth optionality (data-centre connectivity products, Hyperfibre, inter-island subsea cable, battery storage trials) requires Chorus to execute outside its core regulated wholesale-access competency; the shelving of the previously-touted Trans-Tasman Ring project in FY26 shows not every initiative converts to revenue.

financial.risk: High leverage relative to a regulated-utility peer group
financial.description: Net debt/EBITDA was approximately 4.75x at FY26 year-end (net debt $3.2bn, up $72m YoY), close to Chorus' internal 4.75x policy tolerance and within the buffer to the ~5.0-6.0x thresholds typically cited by Moody's and S&P respectively, leaving limited headroom for a downside EBITDA/rate shock. Total equity of $430m at 31 December 2025 against total liabilities of $5.7bn underscores the thin cushion; leverage rose year-on-year even as EBITDA grew, reflecting continued debt-funded capex and dividends exceeding free cash flow generation in some periods.

Total debt of roughly $3.34bn (current $113m + non-current $3,223m at 31 Dec 2025) including EUR and AUD medium-term notes swapped back to NZD; weighted average interest rate was 4.9% in HY26 (down from 5.7% in HY25, with ~70% of floating exposure hedged), but large maturities recur through 2032 (including a new EUR400m note issued Nov 2025 maturing 2032), and higher-for-longer global rates would raise refinancing costs and pressure the payout ratio.

Substantial EUR (EMTN) and AUD (AMTN) debt requires cross-currency interest rate swaps; while fully hedged by policy, this adds counterparty and hedge-effectiveness risk to the balance sheet, and increases finance-expense volatility around refinancing events (e.g., the EUR300m note repurchase at 81.5% of face value and EUR400m reissue completed in HY26).

regulatory.risk: PQ3 cost-of-capital reset (from 2029) trending toward a LOWER allowed WACC
regulatory.description: The 2027 Fibre Input Methodologies Review (Tranche 1 final decision package published 25 August 2026) found a marked reduction in the assessed systematic risk of fibre businesses -- the key input the Commission uses to set allowed WACC. Chorus and fellow LFC Enable have submitted that a higher percentile within the WACC range may be justified given the cost of under-investment, but the direction of travel in the Commission's own preliminary analysis is toward a lower allowed return for PQ3 than PQ2. Final cost-of-capital parameters (Tranche 2 and the cross-sector Common Cost of Capital IM review) are due in Q4 2026; this is a material multi-year valuation swing factor to monitor closely over the next 3-6 months.

The Commerce Commission has signalled it will move to a multi-year (proposed five-year) trailing average to calculate the allowed cost of debt for regulated fibre operators, replacing a single-point-in-time snapshot. This should reduce volatility/refinancing-timing risk in Chorus' allowed revenue and is broadly a neutral-to-mildly-positive structural change, smoothing rather than boosting allowed returns.

The Commerce Commission recommended deregulating copper services outside the fibre footprint in 2025/26, and Chorus brought forward full copper retirement from 2030 to 2028. Copper lines in Chorus' fibre zone are now fewer than 1,000, so most execution risk on this front has already played out; remaining risk is limited to the rural/non-fibre-area retirement through 2028.

regulatory.risk: Government NIFFCo securities sale/monetisation -- now completed
regulatory.description: The NZ Government announced in December 2025 its intention to monetise the National Infrastructure Funding and Financing Co (NIFFCo) debt/securities linked to the original UFB deployment; settlement of the ~$702m sale (a ~$60m gain over the $642m book value) completed in August 2026, funding Crown infrastructure projects (Cambridge-to-Piarere roading, hospital upgrades, classrooms). The transaction did not change Chorus' ownership or the terms and conditions of the underlying securities per both Chorus and Crown statements; this risk is now largely resolved with no material read-through identified to date.

macro.description: Management has flagged a 'challenging' NZ economy in recent commentary; while broadband is a near-essential service, plan downgrades, slower new-connection growth, and payment difficulties among retail customers can flow through to Chorus.

As a highly-levered, long-duration infrastructure asset with a regulator-set allowed return, Chorus' equity value and dividend capacity are directly sensitive to the risk-free rate and the WACC the Commerce Commission allows in each regulatory period -- doubly so given the PQ3 WACC reset is trending toward a lower allowed return (see regulatory risks above).
100% of revenue and assets are in New Zealand, with no geographic diversification to offset a domestic regulatory, macro or political shock.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand's fixed broadband market has substantially completed its transition to fibre (now the dominant fixed technology), with copper retired industry-wide by 2028; growth is now incremental uptake and ARPU mix-shift rather than network build, consistent with global post-UFB fibre telco peers. However, the 'last 25%' of uptake is proving structurally harder, with LEO satellite (Starlink) now the largest single rural broadband provider by connections, a genuinely new competitive dynamic versus the pre-2025 environment.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate — broadband is a near-essential utility service with sticky demand, but new connections/property development activity and discretionary plan upgrades are somewhat sensitive to the NZ economic cycle and housing market.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — Chorus carries roughly NZ$3.2-3.3bn of net/gross debt (~4.5-4.75x net debt/EBITDA) and is valued substantially on dividend yield/regulatory WACC dynamics, making both its cost of capital and its equity valuation directly sensitive to NZ and global interest rates, and to the Commerce Commission's own evolving view of fibre's systematic risk (currently trending toward a lower allowed WACC for PQ3).
key_input_costs: Electricity (network power consumption, partly offset by copper withdrawal energy savings)
Labour and field service company contractor costs
Debt/interest costs on NZD, EUR and AUD borrowings
Network equipment and IT/cloud migration costs

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results: revenue ~$1,020-1,029m (up ~1%); EBITDA $726m (up 3% YoY, upper end of $710-730m guidance); net profit $37m (up from $4m in FY25, a >9x increase); operating cash flow $740m (up 4%); fibre broadband revenue up 6% ($47m increase); free cash flow for capital allocation $368m (up 4% from $354m FY25); fibre uptake reached 75.9% (UFB1 77.3%, UFB2 67.5%); ARPU rose ~2% to $59.51/month; monthly data usage per connection up 9% to 731GB; gross capex $375m (down $35m YoY, sustaining capex $205m, growth capex $170m); copper lines disconnected fell 52% (48,000 lines) leaving fewer than 1,000 in Chorus' fibre zone; net debt $3.2bn (up $72m YoY), net debt/EBITDA ~4.75x; full-year dividend 60 cents/share (24c interim + 36c final, up 4.3% YoY); FY27 minimum dividend guidance of 62 cents/share (up 3.3%), expected to carry partial imputation; FY27 EBITDA guidance $730-760m; new data-centre-adjacent products highlighted (Express Connect live in 8 data centres, Unified Transport, TimeSync in build phase) plus Hyperfibre target of 70,000 connections by 2030 and early-stage inter-island subsea cable/battery storage optionality.

Director William Irving purchased 10,000 Chorus shares on-market for approximately NZ$88,569 (lifting his holding from 45,000 to 55,000 shares), the day after FY26 results -- a modestly positive insider signal. Market reaction to the results was muted-to-slightly-negative on some readings (dividend growth welcomed but debt levels remained a focus for commentators).

The Commerce Commission published its final decision package for Tranche 1 of the 2027 Fibre Input Methodologies Review, covering matters relevant to Chorus' PQ3 (from 2029) price-quality path reset proposal. Separately, the Commission signalled (in preliminary analysis reported mid-September 2026) a marked reduction in the assessed systematic risk of fibre businesses -- a key WACC input -- and proposed moving to a multi-year (five-year) trailing average for the allowed cost of debt. Final cost-of-capital parameters (Tranche 2 plus the cross-sector Common Cost of Capital IM review) are due in Q4 2026.

NZ Finance Minister Nicola Willis and Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop announced the Crown had completed binding agreements to monetise (sell down) the National Infrastructure Funding and Financing Co (NIFFCo) debt it holds in Chorus, originating from interest-free UFB loans made 2012-2023. Net proceeds to the Crown were approximately NZ$702m (a ~$60m gain over the $642m book value); settlement completed during August 2026. Chorus reiterated it does not expect material changes to the terms of the underlying securities.

Chorus confirmed acceleration of full copper network retirement to 2028 (from the prior 2030 target), following the Commerce Commission's 2025 recommendation to deregulate copper access services outside the fibre footprint on the basis that FWA and satellite competition has made copper regulation unnecessary.

HY26 EBITDA rose 3% to $357m (HY25: $346m); revenue $506m (HY25: $500m); net profit swung to $15m (from a $5m loss in HY25); fibre connections grew ~14,000 in the half to 1.129m; fibre uptake reached 72.4%; fibre ARPU rose to $57.73/month; gross capex was $158m, down $41m half-on-half; interim dividend of 24 cents per share declared (up 4% YoY); Chorus issued EUR400m of new 7-year notes (3.529% coupon) and repurchased EUR243m of its EUR300m 2026-maturity notes at 81.5% of face value.

Chorus rural fixed broadband competitive dynamics shifted materially: the Commerce Commission's 2025 Telecommunications Monitoring Report recorded Starlink at 27% of rural broadband connections (up from 19% the year before), overtaking Spark (23%) and One NZ (18%) to become NZ's single largest rural broadband provider.
FY25 net profit returned to $4m (from a $9m FY24 loss); revenue $1.014bn; EBITDA $705m; full-year dividend of 57.5 cents (up 21% YoY); fibre uptake reached ~72%.

items.notes: Up from the FY26 guided range of $710-730m (FY26 actual landed at $726m, upper end). Represents roughly flat-to-modest growth guidance for FY27.

items.target: Minimum 62 cents per share, expected partially imputed
items.notes: Up 3.3% from FY26's 60 cents per share (24c interim + 36c final paid in FY26). The move to partial imputation is a new, incremental positive for NZ resident shareholders' after-tax yield versus the fully unimputed FY26 dividend.

Same range as FY26 guidance; FY26 actual gross capex came in at $375m (bottom of the prior range), down $35m YoY, with sustaining capex $205m and growth capex $170m. FY27 sustaining capex specifically guided at $195-215m.
Continued sharp decline as the network approaches full retirement by end of CY2028; copper lines in Chorus' fibre zone were already fewer than 1,000 at FY26 year-end.

items.target: Not to materially exceed 4.75x in normal circumstances
items.notes: Internal tolerance level; actual was approximately 4.75x at FY26 year-end (net debt $3.2bn, up $72m YoY), i.e. tracking at the policy ceiling rather than with comfortable headroom.

Board considers a BBB-equivalent rating appropriate; rated BBB/positive outlook by S&P and Baa2/stable by Moody's as at the HY26 report (23 Feb 2026). No confirmed rating action identified since; the positive S&P outlook is worth monitoring for a potential upgrade given improving leverage trajectory (FY26 EBITDA growth partly offset by rising absolute net debt).
Fibre-zone copper already down to fewer than 1,000 lines at FY26 year-end; remaining retirement work is concentrated in non-fibre/rural areas through 2028.
New premium gigabit-plus product target disclosed at FY26 results, part of the broader ARPU/data-centre-adjacent growth push.

guidance.management_commentary: At the FY26 result (24 August 2026), management highlighted continued fibre uptake growth (75.9%, though the rural/UFB2 cohort at 67.5% remains the harder-to-convert 'last mile'), ARPU gains (+2% to $59.51), and a 9% increase in average monthly data usage per connection (731GB) as evidence that 'New Zealand's fibre network is already built for the AI era,' with new data-centre-adjacent products (Express Connect, Unified Transport, TimeSync) positioned to capture data-centre and AI-driven demand growth. Management raised FY27 EBITDA guidance to $730-760m and lifted the minimum FY27 dividend to 62 cents (with partial imputation expected), while flagging copper revenue will fall further into the 'high teens' of millions as the network nears full retirement. On competition, management acknowledged opportunities to work with satellite operators on backhaul services even as it competes with them at the retail-substitution level. Leverage (net debt/EBITDA ~4.75x, at the top of Chorus' own policy tolerance) and the ongoing 2027 Fibre IM Review (which could set a lower allowed WACC for PQ3 from 2029) were flagged by analysts and commentators as the key swing factors to watch into FY27-28, alongside the final cost-of-capital determination expected from the Commerce Commission in Q4 2026.

bull_case: Regulated monopoly with multi-year revenue/cash-flow visibility under the PQ2 (2025-2028) framework, now well past the heavy UFB build capex cycle: FY26 free cash flow for capital allocation reached $368m (+4% YoY) even as capex fell to $375m

High and growing dividend (62 cents minimum FY27 guidance, up from 42.5 cents FY22, now expected with partial imputation) under a payout policy (70-90% of net operating FCF) explicitly targeting inflation-linked growth — an attractive, relatively defensive income profile for an infrastructure/utility investor

Copper network is now almost fully retired in Chorus' fibre zone (fewer than 1,000 lines remaining) two years ahead of the original 2030 schedule, delivering the cost-out and margin benefits earlier than modelled, plus a new copper-recycling revenue stream

FY26 net profit rose more than 9x to $37m and EBITDA hit the upper end of guidance at $726m; new AI/data-centre-adjacent revenue lines (Express Connect, Unified Transport, TimeSync, Hyperfibre targeting 70,000 connections by 2030) offer incremental growth optionality beyond the core regulated wholesale business, with monthly data usage per connection up 9% YoY evidencing structural demand tailwinds

Positive insider signal: director William Irving bought $88.6k of shares on-market the day after FY26 results, and S&P maintains a positive outlook on Chorus' BBB rating, suggesting potential for a credit upgrade if leverage stabilises
bear_case: Leverage is tracking at the top of Chorus' own policy tolerance (~4.75x net debt/EBITDA, net debt $3.2bn and rising $72m YoY in FY26 despite EBITDA growth), leaving little room for a downside surprise (regulatory, rate, or EBITDA), and a large EUR/AUD-denominated debt stack recurs through 2032, creating ongoing refinancing and interest-rate risk

PQ3 (from 2029) is trending toward a LOWER allowed WACC, not a higher one: the Commerce Commission's own preliminary analysis for the 2027 Fibre IM Review found a marked reduction in fibre's assessed systematic risk, and final cost-of-capital parameters due Q4 2026 are a material, near-term valuation swing factor that could cap or reduce Chorus' allowed returns for the next regulatory period

Fixed wireless (5G) and Starlink/LEO satellite are no longer just a future threat -- Starlink has already overtaken Spark and One NZ to become New Zealand's single largest rural broadband provider by connections (27% share, up from 19%), directly validating the substitution risk the Commerce Commission cited to justify copper deregulation and capping fibre's realistic uptake ceiling in the hardest-to-convert 'last 25%' of the footprint (UFB2 uptake lags at 67.5% vs 77.3% in UFB1)

Interest-rate sensitive equity valuation: as a high-payout, high-leverage bond-proxy stock, CNU is vulnerable to a higher-for-longer global rate environment compressing the relative attractiveness of its dividend yield; naive P/E screens are still distorted by heavy D&A and interest expense against a much larger EBITDA base, even with FY26 net profit recovering to $37m

New growth initiatives (data-centre products, Hyperfibre, inter-island subsea cable, battery storage trials) carry real execution risk outside Chorus' core regulated-wholesale competency, as demonstrated by the shelving of the previously-touted Trans-Tasman Ring project in FY26; analysts have flagged 'debt, copper drag and execution risk' as the key offset to the positive fibre-uptake and dividend story
